headline: Oil-driven pullback cools into a loaded Fed-and-earnings week
body: Friday's close capped a choppy week: the Dow fell roughly 1.2% to 52,215, the S&P 500 slipped about 0.5% to 7,624, and the Nasdaq held nearly flat at 25,955 after steadying from Thursday's sharp chip-led drop, its worst single session since June. The proximate driver was oil, which pushed above $100 a barrel on renewed fears of a US-Iran flare-up over the Strait of Hormuz, hitting consumer staples, utilities, and healthcare harder than growth names — an inversion of the usual risk-off script, where defensive sectors typically hold up best. American Express sliding more than 3% on job-cut news added to the cross-currents. For the week, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq each logged a second straight weekly loss even as the Dow still finished higher, a split that reads more as rotation and indecision than a clean, broad-based flight from risk.

The coming week carries the real catalysts. The Fed's October 27-28 meeting is widely expected to hold rates at 3.75%-4.00% despite September inflation running at 3.7% year-over-year, leaving the debate over a possible December move unresolved. Right behind it comes one of the heaviest stretches of mega-cap tech earnings this quarter — Microsoft and Alphabet due Wednesday, Amazon and Intel Thursday — which will test whether AI capital spending is translating into results after two down weeks for growth-heavy indices. Retail-sentiment chatter was thin and inconclusive in today's search, so this read leans more on price action, oil, and the Fed/earnings calendar than on social-media positioning. Taken together, the setup looks like a market pausing to digest a stretched AI-led run rather than one in genuine distress — cautious and headline-reactive, but not fearful.
